opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think of it as a loop, and the key is closing that loop as tightly as possible. On the digital side, you have generative models that propose candidate structures, and then a whole hierarchy of simulators to evaluate them: very cheap machine-learned surrogates at the top, then more expensive things like DFT, and maybe even higher-fidelity quantum chemistry at the bottom. You use the cheap tools to search an enormous space and the expensive ones to verify the most promising candidates.

But at some point you have to touch reality. Simulations have systematic errors, and some properties you care about, like stability over thousands of cycles or how a material behaves in a real device, are just very hard to simulate. So the experiment becomes another, very expensive, very high-fidelity oracle in that hierarchy. The question is how to spend that budget wisely. That's where ideas like active learning and Bayesian experimental design come in: you choose the experiment that tells you the most, not just the one you think will work best.

And the data that comes back from the lab shouldn't just be a yes or no. It should flow back and recalibrate your models, so the simulators and the generative model learn where they're wrong. Over time the whole system gets better at predicting what will actually work in the lab.

I also think, honestly, the bottleneck is increasingly on the physical side. Generating candidates is getting cheap. Synthesizing them, characterizing them, and scaling them up is still slow. So automated labs and robotics, and also learning to predict synthesizability, are going to matter a lot. Otherwise you end up with a beautiful list of materials that nobody can make.

The way I like to put it: the computer is the imagination, and the experiment is the reality check. You need both talking to each other constantly. That's how I think we'll get to things like better carbon capture materials or batteries on the time scales the climate problem actually requires.

r001.rationale: The response describes experiments as a high-fidelity oracle and reality check, but does not frame them as computations performed by nature.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really the thing I've been obsessed with for the last few years. The way I think about it is that nature is actually a computer. If you want to know what a molecule does, or how a material behaves, you can try to simulate it, but the simulation is always an approximation of reality. The physical experiment is reality. So why not use it as a compute resource?

The problem is that the two have historically lived in completely different worlds. On the digital side you have very fast, very cheap, but imprecise computation: density functional theory, molecular dynamics, and now all these machine-learned force fields and generative models that can propose millions of candidate structures in an afternoon. On the physical side you have the lab, which is slow, expensive, and noisy, but it's the ground truth. And the way most of science has worked is that a human sits in between, reads papers, has a hunch, runs a few experiments, goes back to the whiteboard. That loop is incredibly slow.

What I think is happening now is that we can close that loop and take the human off the critical path, or at least move them up a level. You have a model, the model proposes a batch of candidates, you synthesize and characterize them in a self-driving lab, the results come back, you update the model, and you go again. It's active learning in the most literal sense. And the interesting thing is that the model doesn't just learn about the materials, it learns where its own simulations are wrong. So the digital side gets calibrated against reality in a very targeted way.

There are a couple of things that make this hard, though, and I don't want to pretend it's solved. One is that the physical world has a very different cost structure. In digital you can sample a million points for free. In the lab every sample costs you hours and real money, so the question of which experiment to run becomes the whole game. That's a Bayesian experimental design problem, and I think that's where a lot of the real intellectual action is, not in the generative model per se.

The second is that the data you get back is messy. An experiment fails for all kinds of mundane reasons, a pipette clogged, the humidity was off, and you need your models to be robust to that and to actually learn the failure modes of the lab as well.

And then the third thing, which I find really exciting from a physics point of view, is that you want the models in the middle to respect what we already know. We know energy is conserved, we know there are symmetries, rotations, translations, permutations of identical atoms. If you bake those into the architecture you need far fewer experiments to learn something useful. That was really the motivation behind a lot of the equivariant network work. You're not throwing away three hundred years of physics, you're using it as an inductive bias so that the expensive physical data goes a lot further.

So the short version is: the digital side proposes and extrapolates, the physical side verifies and corrects, and the whole thing becomes one learning system. And I genuinely think that's how we're going to find the next battery electrolyte or the next catalyst, not by a human having a brilliant idea, but by this loop running a thousand times faster than a human could.

r001.rationale: The candidate says “nature is actually a computer” and proposes using physical experiments as a compute resource.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting opportunity is to make this a closed loop. You have a model that proposes a material, but then you have to make it and measure its properties. Those measurements come back into the model, and that informs the next experiment. So computation and experimentation become parts of one learning process.

The key question is: which experiment should you do next? It’s not necessarily the material that your model predicts will perform best. It might be one where the model is uncertain, and where a measurement would teach you something useful. You have to balance improving the material with improving your understanding.

Physics gives you a very useful starting point. We know about symmetries, conservation laws, and interactions, and we can build some of that structure into our models. But simulations are approximations, and making a material in the lab introduces things the model may not capture. The experiment is what keeps the whole process grounded.

So I would think of this as a collaboration between a predictive model and an experimental system, with scientists deciding what matters and interpreting what comes back. The goal is to make each expensive physical experiment more informative.

r001.rationale: The response describes experiments as measurements that feed a learning loop, but does not frame nature or physical experiments as computations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting opportunity is to close the loop between computation and experiment. You build a model that predicts properties of materials, use it to propose promising candidates, then actually make those materials and measure them. Those measurements feed back into the model, and you repeat.

The important question is which experiment to do next. You don’t necessarily want to test only the material your model thinks is best. You also want experiments that resolve uncertainty, because that can improve all your subsequent predictions. So there’s a balance between looking for a useful material and learning something about the space of possibilities.

Physics gives you a very valuable starting point. You can build symmetries and other constraints into the model, and use simulations where they’re reliable. But experiments keep the process grounded: a material might look wonderful in a simulation and turn out to be difficult to synthesize, or behave differently under real conditions.

So I would think of the digital and physical parts as one learning system. The computation helps decide what to measure, and the measurements tell you where the computation needs to improve.

r001.rationale: The response describes experiments as measurements that validate and improve computational models, but it does not frame physical experiments as computations performed by nature.
